idiom_name: Proc/lambda rules composed with Proc#>> (or reduced with all?); Dry::Validation contracts
implementation_notes: A validator is a lambda or Proc (->(cfg) { (1..65_535).cover?(cfg[:port]) }) and Ruby's Proc#>> and Proc#<< are function composition, so contramap is a projection composed with a rule (PROJECT >> RULE), divide is reducing a rule array with all? - or reject/map when every failing rule must be reported - and choose is a case/in pattern match on a class or hash shape. Method objects (obj.method(:check)) are callables too, so rules can live as instance methods without a wrapper class. For schema-level validation the community answer is dry-validation: Dry::Validation::Contract with params/schema blocks and rule blocks evaluates all rules and returns errors keyed by path instead of one boolean.
code_sketch:
NON_EMPTY = ->(s) { !s.to_s.empty? }                    # rule
HOST_OK   = ->(cfg) { cfg[:host] } >> NON_EMPTY         # contramap via Proc#>>
RULES = [HOST_OK, ->(cfg) { (1..65_535).cover?(cfg[:port]) }]
failed = RULES.reject { |rule| rule.call(cfg) }         # no short-circuit: all failures

class ConfigContract < Dry::Validation::Contract         # declarative, path-keyed errors
  rule(:port) { key.failure("must be 1..65535") unless (1..65_535).cover?(value) }
end
pitfalls: Proc#>> composes left-to-right while Proc#<< composes right-to-left: mixing them in one rule file silently inverts a check, so pick one direction and keep it.
Lambdas check arity and procs do not: a rule that must take exactly one argument should be a lambda (->), otherwise a mis-composed pipeline fails late inside the rule.
Only nil and false are falsy in Ruby, so a rule returning 0, '' or an empty array counts as success - make rules return explicit booleans.
